event: A 3-day ice storm began that left over 200,000 southwest Missourians without power.
takeaway: Run a generator only outdoors, 20 feet or more from windows, doors and garages.
event_quote: The Historic January 12-14 Ice Storm left over 200,000 southwest Missourians without power and a landscape resembling a war zone.
takeaway_quote: Generators and fuel should always be used outdoors and at least 20 feet away from windows, doors and attached garages.

event: An ice storm began, coating much of Kansas with 1 to 4 inches of ice.
takeaway: In an outage keep the freezer shut; a full one holds its temperature about 48 hours.
event_quote: January 29-31, 2002: Southwest, South-Central, and all of Eastern Kansas. Sleet and freezing rain caused horrific 1-4 inch ice accumulations across most areas.
takeaway_quote: Keep freezers and refrigerators closed. The refrigerator will keep food cold for about four hours. A full freezer will keep the temperature for about 48 hours.

place: Kansas City and the I-70 corridor
event: A blizzard dropped 12-18 inches along I-70, forcing its first-ever statewide closure.
takeaway: Stranded? Stay in the car. Run it 10 min an hour, exhaust clear, window cracked.
event_quote: Nearby, an equally impressive snowfall of 12-18 inches fell along the Interstate 70 corridor, causing the first ever state-wide closure of Interstate 70 from Tuesday night into early Wednesday.
takeaway_quote: Run the motor about 10 minutes each hour for heat. While running the motor, open the window a little for fresh air to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning. Clear snow from the exhaust pipe to avoid gas poisoning.

event: Freezing drizzle iced roads in eastern Kansas and western Missouri; at least 3 died.
takeaway: Even a thin glaze is deadly. Bridges and overpasses ice over first.
event_quote: At least three fatalities were caused by the icy roads on February 5, one in Miami County Kansas, and two in Lafayette County Missouri.
takeaway_quote: Even small accumulations of ice can be extremely dangerous to motorists and pedestrians. Bridges and overpasses are particularly dangerous because they freeze before other surfaces.

event: A historic Arctic outbreak began on the Plains and lasted through February 18.
takeaway: Before deep cold, seal drafts and learn how to keep your pipes from freezing.
event_quote: An historic cold outbreak overspread all of the Plains on February 6th and lasted through February 18th.
takeaway_quote: Prepare your home to keep out the cold with insulation, caulking and weather stripping. Learn how to keep pipes from freezing.

event: A great earthquake destroyed New Madrid and threw down chimneys in St. Louis.
takeaway: Secure bookcases, water heaters and TVs now, before the shaking starts.
event_quote: Several destructive shocks occurred on February 7, the last of which equaled or surpassed the magnitude of any previous event. The town of New Madrid was destroyed. At St. Louis, many houses were damaged severely and their chimneys were thrown down.
takeaway_quote: Protect Your Home: Secure heavy items in your home like bookcases, refrigerators, water heaters, televisions and objects that hang on walls.

event: Tornadoes struck Urich, Sedalia and Renick, Missouri, killing 6 and injuring 49.
takeaway: Tornadoes can strike in March. Pick and practice your shelter spot early.
event_quote: Unfortunately, 6 lives were lost from the tornadoes that struck Urich, Sedalia and Renick, Missouri. Another 49 persons were injured.
takeaway_quote: Identify and practice going to a safe shelter such as a safe room built using FEMA criteria or a storm shelter built to ICC 500 standards.

event: An ice storm cut power to about 100,000 people in Topeka, 82% of the city.
takeaway: Keep a working flashlight for every person in your home before ice season.
event_quote: Topeka was hit especially hard as the heavy weight of the ice severed power to around 100,000 people, or about 82% of the city’s population.
takeaway_quote: Have flashlights for every household member.

event: The Andover F5 tornado killed 17; 13 of them died in one mobile home park.
takeaway: Mobile homes are not safe in a tornado. Know the sturdy building you'll go to.
event_quote: It roared into Andover, drawing a bead on the Golden Spur mobile home park which was devastated. It was at the mobile home park where 13 of the 17 fatalities occurred.
takeaway_quote: Outside: Seek shelter inside a sturdy building immediately if a tornado is approaching. Sheds and storage facilities are not safe. Neither is a mobile home or tent.

event: Rain of up to around 12 inches began in the Missouri Ozarks, destroying roads and bridges.
takeaway: Stay off bridges over fast-moving water. Floods can wash them out without warning.
event_quote: Storm total rainfall amounts generally ranged from 4 to 8 inches with some areas of far southern and south central Missouri receiving from 10 to around 12 inches. This incredible rainfall resulted in widespread and historic flooding. Numerous roads, bridges and buildings were destroyed.
takeaway_quote: Stay off bridges over fast-moving water. Fast-moving water can wash bridges away without warning.

event: A 1.7-mile-wide tornado destroyed 95% of Greensburg, killing 11 and injuring 60.
takeaway: In a tornado warning, go to a basement, safe room or interior room away from windows.
event_quote: Estimated to be 1.7 miles in width, the tornado was wider than the town of Greensburg itself. Ninety-five percent of the town was destroyed within minutes, with 60 people injured, and 11 killed.
takeaway_quote: At Your House: If you are in a tornado warning, go to your basement, safe room, or an interior room away from windows.

event: The Ruskin Heights tornado killed 44 people, 37 in Missouri, and injured 531.
takeaway: No basement? Arrange now to shelter with a neighbor who has one.
event_quote: The human toll was significant, 44 people lost their lives, 7 in Kansas and 37 in Missouri, and 531 people were injured.
takeaway_quote: Because of warnings on radio and television, many Ruskin Heights residents were able to take refuge in their basements or with neighbors who had basements.

event: An EF5 tornado struck Joplin, killing 158 people and injuring over 1,000.
takeaway: Act on the first warning; don't wait for more proof before you shelter.
event_quote: On May 22, 2011, one of the deadliest tornadoes in United States history struck Joplin, Missouri, directly killing 158 people and injuring over 1,000.
takeaway_quote: The majority of Joplin residents did not immediately take protective action upon receiving a first indication of risk (usually via the local siren system), regardless of the source of the warning.
checked: 2026-11-26 independent re-fetch: keep; 2026-11-26 review: reworded to drop blame, per its own quote

event: The Udall tornado killed 80 people, the deadliest tornado in Kansas history.
takeaway: Warnings can come at night. A NOAA weather radio broadcasts 24 hours a day.
event_quote: The tornado also killed 5 children 3 miles northeast of Oxford, bringing the total number of fatalities to 80. It is still the deadliest tornado in Kansas history.
takeaway_quote: NWR broadcasts official Weather Service warnings, watches, forecasts and other hazard information 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

event: An F5 tornado cut through Topeka, killing 17 people and injuring over 500.
takeaway: Get to the lowest floor, with as many walls as possible between you and outside.
event_quote: The massive 1966 Topeka tornado killed 17 people, injured over 500 and caused over $200 million damage; at the time, the highest in America history.
takeaway_quote: Remember to get to the lowest floor of a home or building and to get as many walls between you and the outside as possible.

event: The 'Inland Hurricane' hit six Kansas counties with 65 to 120 mph straight-line winds.
takeaway: Treat severe thunderstorm warnings seriously: get inside to an interior room.
event_quote: One of the most destructive storms in South Central Kansas history swept through on June 19th 1990 and would later be titled the “Inland Hurricane”. This storm produced a large swath of 65 to 120 mph straight line winds through parts of six counties causing over $80 million dollars damage.
takeaway_quote: Immediately go inside a sturdy building during a high wind warning or severe thunderstorm warning and move to an interior room or basement.

place: Kansas River valley, Manhattan to Bonner Springs
event: The Kansas River crested 4-6 feet over all prior records, Manhattan to Bonner Springs, KS.
takeaway: Check FEMA's flood maps for your address, then remember water ignores map lines.
event_quote: On July 13, the Kansas River crested at all official gaging stations, from Manhattan to Bonner Springs, at 4 to 6 feet above all previous recorded crests.
takeaway_quote: Know your risk for floods, visit FEMA's Flood Map Service Center to know types of flood risks in your area. However, remember that flooding doesn’t follow lines on a map.

event: A windstorm with gusts over 70 mph knocked out power to nearly 200,000 in the KC metro.
takeaway: Treat every downed power line as live. Stay well away and report it.
event_quote: Numerous wind reports, both estimated and measured were over 70 mph. At one point nearly 200,000 people across the Kansas City metro lost power.
takeaway_quote: Keep in mind that power lines that are laying on the ground may be live. Do not go near them!

event: Rain began over KC around 9 pm; overnight floods trapped two restaurant owners in rafters.
takeaway: Trapped by rising water indoors? Go to the highest level, never a closed attic.
event_quote: Also at that intersection was a restaurant that had two of its owners trapped in the rafters of the business as waters rushed into the building.
takeaway_quote: Get to the highest level if trapped in a building. Only get on the roof if necessary and once there, signal for help. Do not climb into a closed attic to avoid getting trapped by rising floodwater.

event: The Great Flood of 1993 crested at 49.58 feet on the Mississippi River at St. Louis.
takeaway: Homeowner policies don't cover floods. Flood insurance takes up to 30 days to start.
event_quote: This flood evolved from a series of heavy rain events along the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers, culminating with a crest of 49.58 feet and a flow of 1.08 million cubic feet per second on August 1 on the Mississippi River at St. Louis.
takeaway_quote: Homeowner’s insurance policies do not cover flooding. It typically takes up to 30 days for a policy to go into effect, so the time to buy is well before a disaster.

event: Wichita hit 114 degrees, its all-time record high temperature.
takeaway: In a heat wave, check daily on older, sick or frail neighbors.
event_quote: The all-time record high temperature of 114 degrees was set on August 12, 1936 at Wichita.
takeaway_quote: Check on older, sick, or frail people who may need help responding to the heat.

event: A KC-area heat wave began; heat indices reached 120-130, and 134 in Lawrence, Kansas.
takeaway: Fans alone won't prevent heat illness. Find air conditioning or a cooling center.
event_quote: The combination of the extreme heat and the excessively high dewpoints led to heat indices from August 19 through August 25 to rise to 120-130 degrees. The hottest heat index in the area occurred in Lawrence, Kansas on the 20th and 21st, when it rose to 134 degrees.
takeaway_quote: Do not rely on a fan as your primary cooling device. Fans create air flow and a false sense of comfort, but do not reduce body temperature or prevent heat-related illnesses.

event: Heavy rain flooded the KC metro; overnight, one person died in deep rushing water.
takeaway: Never walk or drive into flood water. A foot of moving water can sweep a car away.
event_quote: Several water rescues were made overnight Monday into Tuesday morning, with one fatality due to flooding. The fatality occurred on the east side of HWY 69 near 363rd St in Miami County, where deep rushing water was present.
takeaway_quote: Never drive around barricades. Local responders use them to safely direct traffic out of flooded areas.

place: Country Club Plaza, Kansas City, Missouri
event: The Plaza flash flood in Kansas City killed 25 people; 17 of them were in vehicles.
takeaway: Never drive into flood water. Just 12 inches of rushing water can carry off a car.
event_quote: Of the 25 fatalities occurring from this event, 17 were in vehicles, and 20 were in Missouri.
takeaway_quote: It takes just 12 inches of rushing water to carry away most cars and just 2 feet of rushing water can carry away SUVs and trucks.

event: A tornado tore into downtown St. Louis, ripping apart over 200 city blocks.
takeaway: At work, know your shelter spot. Avoid windows and big open rooms.
event_quote: In downtown St. Louis, the path widened from 100 to 600 yards, with microburst damage extending out over a mile wide. Over 200 city blocks were torn apart.
takeaway_quote: At Your Workplace or School: Follow your tornado drill and proceed to your tornado shelter location quickly and calmly. Stay away from windows and do not go to large open rooms such as cafeterias, gymnasiums, or auditoriums.

event: KC flash floods killed 11; ten died after sunset in vehicles, eight at Brush Creek.
takeaway: Flood water can be deeper than it looks and hide a washed-out road. Turn around.
event_quote: Flash flooding along Brush Creek, Turkey Creek and Indian Creek resulted in eleven people losing their lives - eight lives alone were claimed as Brush Creek inundated the Prospect Road bridge. Ten of the eleven deaths occurred after sunset and in automobiles
takeaway_quote: Water may be deeper than it appears and can hide hazards such as sharp objects, washed out road surfaces, electrical wires, chemicals, etc.

event: The Halloween flood began: 6 to 10-plus inches of rain fell in south-central Kansas.
takeaway: If officials order an evacuation, leave right away. Don't wait for the water.
event_quote: Friday evening on the 30th of Oct 1998 was the start of a long weekend of widespread flooding rains impacting central and southeast Kansas. Rainfall amounts of 4-8 inches were common in Central Kansas, with 6-10 plus inches being recorded across South Central and Southeast parts of the state.
takeaway_quote: Obey Evacuation Orders: If told to evacuate, do so immediately.

event: An early blizzard dropped 5.8 inches, KC's snowiest November 25 on record.
takeaway: Winterize your vehicle and pack a winter survival kit before the season starts.
event_quote: The 5.8" of snow broke the record for snowiest November 25 in Kansas City history.
takeaway_quote: Fully check and winterize your vehicle before the winter season begins. Carry a Winter Storm Survival Kit

event: An ice storm cut power to about 260,000 people in Kansas, some for up to 2 weeks.
takeaway: Outages bring generators and heaters. Put battery-backup CO detectors on every level.
event_quote: Around 260,000 people lost power many of them were in the dark for up to 2 weeks.
takeaway_quote: Install carbon monoxide detectors with battery backup in central locations on every level of your home.

event: Kansas City fell to 23 below zero, its coldest temperature on record.
takeaway: A body temperature below 95 degrees is an emergency. Know hypothermia's signs.
event_quote: Kansas City: Average winter snowfall (Oct-Apr, 1981-2010): 18.8" Warmest winter season (Dec-Feb): 37.1 degrees (1991-1992) Coldest winter season (Dec-Feb): 21.5 degrees (1978-1979) Coldest temperature ever recorded: -23 degrees on Dec. 22 and 23, 1989
takeaway_quote: Hypothermia is an unusually low body temperature. A temperature below 95 degrees is an emergency.

event: President Grant signed the law creating a national weather service to warn of storms.
takeaway: NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts official warnings 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
event_quote: Congress passed the resolution and on February 9, 1870, President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law. A new national weather service had been born
takeaway_quote: NWR broadcasts official warnings, watches, forecasts and other hazard information 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

event: The first 911 call in the US connected to the police station in Haleyville, Alabama.
takeaway: Keep 911 for emergencies; non-emergency calls can delay help for people who need it.
event_quote: At 2:00 p.m. on February 16, 1968, the speaker of the Alabama House of Representatives, Rankin Fite, dialed 911. He was connected to the Haleyville, Alabama, police station
takeaway_quote: Using 9-1-1 for non-emergency calls may delay help for people caught in real emergencies.

event: Satellite images showed Texas outages after Arctic cold left millions without power.
takeaway: Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven; it raises carbon monoxide risk.
event_quote: The storm brought frigid temperatures, some of the lowest in decades, which crippled electric grids and left millions without power in several states.
takeaway_quote: Do not use a gas stove or oven to heat your home. It increases your risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.

event: The Blizzard of 1888 began; Albany, NY got 46.7 inches of snow.
takeaway: Gather supplies so you can stay home for several days without power.
event_quote: Total snowfall for the storm was 46.7 inches, but the drifts were significantly higher.
takeaway_quote: Gather supplies in case you need to stay home for several days without power.

event: The 1993 Superstorm began; most of its 300 deaths were heart attacks from shoveling snow.
takeaway: Pace yourself shoveling snow; overexertion raises the risk of a heart attack.
event_quote: The system was responsible for 300 deaths and power outages to over 10 million customers. Most of the deaths were due to heart attacks from shoveling snow.
takeaway_quote: Reduce the risk of a heart attack by avoiding overexertion when shoveling snow and walking in the snow.

event: The Tri-State Tornado killed 695 people across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana.
takeaway: Know tornado signs: a rotating funnel, a debris cloud, or a roar like a freight train.
event_quote: In the aftermath, the death toll mounted to 695 people—at least 71 of those were in Southwest Indiana.
takeaway_quote: Know the signs of a tornado , including a rotating, funnel-shaped cloud, an approaching cloud of debris, or a loud roar like a freight train.

event: Tinker AFB forecasters issued the first official tornado forecast; one hit that evening.
takeaway: A watch means severe weather is possible; a warning means it is seen or expected soon.
event_quote: The first tornado forecast occurred on the evening of March 25, 1948, when a tornado roared through Tinker Air Force Base, causing considerable damage, a few injuries, but no fatalities.
takeaway_quote: A "watch" means severe weather is possible during the next few hours, while a "warning" means that severe weather has been observed, or is expected soon.

event: The magnitude 9.2 Great Alaska Earthquake set off tsunamis that caused 124 of 139 deaths.
takeaway: In a tsunami area, go high and inland once the shaking stops; don't wait for a warning.
event_quote: Of the 139 deaths attributed to this event, 124 were directly caused by the tsunamis.
takeaway_quote: When the shaking stops, if there are natural signs or official warnings of a tsunami, move immediately to a safe place as high and as far inland as possible. Listen to the authorities, but do not wait for tsunami warnings and evacuation orders.

event: A tsunami hit Hilo Bay; 159 people died across Hawaii.
takeaway: Tsunami signs: a loud ocean roar, a sudden rise, or water draining off the sea floor.
event_quote: Yet on Monday, April 1, 1946, a tsunami hit Hilo Bay just before 7 a.m., killing 96 people in 2 hours. A total of 159 people died throughout the state
takeaway_quote: Learn the signs of a potential tsunami, such as an earthquake, a loud roar from the ocean, or unusual ocean behavior, such as a sudden rise or wall of water or sudden draining of water showing the ocean floor.

event: The Super Outbreak began; 148 tornadoes struck 13 states over two days.
takeaway: Sign up for local alerts, and learn your community's siren warning tone.
event_quote: The April 3-4, 1974 Super Outbreak affected 13 states across the eastern United States, from the Great Lakes region all the way to the Deep South. In all, 148 tornadoes were documented from this event
takeaway_quote: Sign up for your community’s warning system. The Emergency Alert System (EAS) and NOAA Weather Radio also provide emergency alerts . If your community has sirens, become familiar with the warning tone.

event: The Palm Sunday tornado outbreak killed 271 in the Midwest; many never got the warnings.
takeaway: Keep a NOAA Weather Radio with a tone alert in your emergency kit.
event_quote: This outbreak ranks as one of the deadliest in recorded history with 271 fatalities and over 3400 injured.
takeaway_quote: Battery-powered or hand crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert

event: A great earthquake struck just after 5:12 a.m. and spawned a fire in San Francisco.
takeaway: After a quake, watch for leaking gas lines and downed power lines.
event_quote: In the public's mind, this earthquake is perhaps remembered most for the fire it spawned in San Francisco
takeaway_quote: There can be serious hazards after an earthquake, such as damage to the building, leaking gas and water lines or downed power lines.

event: A tornado outbreak tore through Alabama; 240 people died in Central Alabama.
takeaway: Pick your shelter now: a basement or small interior windowless room on the lowest floor.
event_quote: There were at least 1998 injuries reported and 240 people lost their lives.
takeaway_quote: The next best protection is a small, interior, windowless room or basement on the lowest level of a sturdy building.

event: Mount St. Helens erupted in Washington, killing 57 people.
takeaway: Avoid driving in heavy ashfall; ash can clog engines and stall vehicles.
event_quote: The May 18 eruption resulted in scores of injuries and the loss of 57 lives.
takeaway_quote: Avoid driving in heavy ash. Driving will stir up volcanic ash that can clog engines and stall vehicles.

event: A solar flare jammed US and UK radar; Air Force forecasters showed the sun was the cause.
takeaway: NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center emails alerts and warnings; you can subscribe.
event_quote: In the middle of the cold war, a massive solar radio burst associated with a powerful solar flare jammed several U.S. and United Kingdom radar and radio communications systems in polar regions.
takeaway_quote: SWPC provides a wide range of alerts, warnings, watches and forecasts you can receive through e-mail within moments of being issued.

event: A dam failed above Johnstown, Pennsylvania; the flood and fires killed 2,209 people.
takeaway: If you live in a flood-prone area and are told to evacuate, go immediately.
event_quote: Historical reports indicate that there were a couple hours of warning given; but few people heeded the calls to move to higher ground, resulting in one of the greatest losses of human life in United State history. The flood and subsequent fires killed 2,209 people
takeaway_quote: Obey Evacuation Orders: If told to evacuate, do so immediately.

event: A derecho knocked 17 call centers offline; over 2 million people could not reach 911.
takeaway: Set a family meeting place in case phones fail and you can't reach each other.
event_quote: Seventeen PSAPs in three states lost service completely, affecting the ability of more than 2 million people to reach 9-1-1 at all.
takeaway_quote: Know how you’ll contact one another and reconnect if separated. Establish a family meeting place that’s familiar and easy to find.

event: A blackout hit 9 million people in New York City; outages lasted up to 26 hours.
takeaway: Keep a flashlight for every person in your household.
event_quote: This disturbance resulted in the loss of 6,000 MW of load and affected 9 million people in New York City. Outages lasted for up to 26 hours.
takeaway_quote: Have flashlights for every household member.

event: A heat wave peaked in Chicago; it killed over 500 people in the city alone.
takeaway: In extreme heat, check on family members, older adults and neighbors.
event_quote: The heat wave claimed over 500 lives in the city of Chicago alone and hundreds more across the Midwest.
takeaway_quote: Check on family members, older adults and neighbors.

event: The Big Thompson Canyon flash flood killed 144 people in Colorado.
takeaway: In a flash flood, walk or climb to higher ground out of low spots and drainages.
event_quote: The Big Thompson Canyon flood of July 31, 1976 was Colorado's worst flash flood in terms of lives lost. That single event claimed 144 lives.
takeaway_quote: If you are in a drainage area or in other low spots, walk or climb to higher ground.

event: A western grid blackout affected 7.5 million people across the West.
takeaway: If you rely on powered medical devices or cold medicines, make an outage plan now.
event_quote: This disturbance resulted in the loss of over 28,000 MW of load and affected 7.5 million people in the West.
takeaway_quote: Have alternate plans for refrigerating medicines or using power-dependent medical devices.

event: A blackout hit an area of about 50 million people in the Midwest, Northeast and Ontario.
takeaway: Keep the fridge shut: food stays cold about 4 hours, a full freezer about 48.
event_quote: On August 14, 2003, large portions of the Midwest and Northeast United States and Ontario, Canada, experienced an electric power blackout. The outage affected an area with an estimated 50 million people
takeaway_quote: The refrigerator will keep food cold for about four hours. A full freezer will keep the temperature for about 48 hours.

event: Hurricane Andrew hit South Florida near Homestead with winds up to 165 mph.
takeaway: For hurricane winds, shelter in a designated storm shelter or an interior room.
event_quote: After briefly weakening, Andrew regained category 5 status with winds up to 165 mph on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale. The hurricane made landfall on Elliott Key , Florida, and then near Homestead on the morning of August 24.
takeaway_quote: Take refuge in a designated storm shelter or an interior room for high winds.

event: Hurricane Harvey made landfall near Port Aransas, Texas, as a Category 4.
takeaway: Never drive into flood water; 12 inches of rushing water can carry away most cars.
event_quote: Harvey made landfall along the Texas coast near Port Aransas around 10:00 p.m. on August 25th as a cat 4 and brought devastating impacts.
takeaway_quote: It takes just 12 inches of rushing water to carry away most cars and just 2 feet of rushing water can carry away SUVs and trucks.

event: Hurricane Katrina struck; storm surge reached 25 to 28 feet on the Mississippi coast.
takeaway: If trapped by flooding, go to the highest level, but never into a closed attic.
event_quote: Storm surge flooding of 25 to 28 feet above normal tide level occurred along portions of the Mississippi coast
takeaway_quote: Go to the highest level of the building if you are trapped by flooding. Do not climb into a closed attic. You may become trapped by rising flood water.

event: Astronomers saw a giant solar flare; its storm later shocked telegraph operators.
takeaway: Space weather can cut power; keep spare batteries or chargers for your phone.
event_quote: Powerful electrical currents flowed through telegraph machine wires, causing them to shock their operators
takeaway_quote: Keep extra batteries or external chargers to charge your phone, laptop and other small electronics in the event of a power outage.

event: The Labor Day hurricane hit the Florida Keys at 185 mph, the strongest US landfall.
takeaway: Learn your evacuation routes and practice them with your household and pets.
event_quote: 1935 – Labor Day hurricane made landfall in Long Key with an intensity of 185 mph, making it a category 5 hurricane, late on September 2nd. This is the strongest hurricane landfall recorded in the United States.
takeaway_quote: You may have to evacuate quickly due to a hurricane if you live in an evacuation zone. Learn your evacuation routes , practice with your household and pets, and identify where you will stay.

event: A Category 4 hurricane hit Galveston, Texas, killing 6,000 to 12,000 people.
takeaway: If you're in an evacuation zone and officials tell you to go, leave immediately.
event_quote: A Category 4 storm made landfall in Galveston, Texas on this day in 1900. This hurricane killed between 6,000 and 12,000 individuals, making it the deadliest US Atlantic hurricane on record.
takeaway_quote: If you live in a mandatory evacuation zone and local officials tell you to evacuate, do so immediately.

event: A hurricane hit Long Island and New England, much stronger than forecasters expected.
takeaway: Have several ways to receive alerts, including the FEMA app, WEA and EAS.
event_quote: This advisory now called the hurricane a tropical storm and had it centered 75 miles from Cape Hatteras. It was actually further away from Cape Hatteras than written in the advisory. The storm was also much larger and stronger than anticipated.
takeaway_quote: Be sure to have several ways to receive alerts.

event: The Peshtigo forest fire swept northeast Wisconsin, claiming over 1,200 lives.
takeaway: Learn your wildfire evacuation routes and where you will go before fire season.
event_quote: On October 8, 1871, the most devastating forest fire in American history swept through northeast Wisconsin, claiming 1200+ lives.
takeaway_quote: You may have to evacuate quickly due to a wildfire. Learn your evacuation routes , practice with pets and identify where you will go.

event: The magnitude 6.9 Loma Prieta earthquake severely shook the San Francisco Bay Area.
takeaway: After a quake, text instead of calling; texts may get through and save battery.
event_quote: On October 17, 1989, at 5:04 PM (PDT), a magnitude 6.9 earthquake severely shook the San Francisco and Monterey Bay regions.
takeaway_quote: Use text messages to communicate. This may be more reliable than phone calls and can save batter power.

event: Extreme solar storms disrupted satellites, GPS and radio, with auroras seen in Texas.
takeaway: Space weather can cause power outages; keep your gas tank at least half full.
event_quote: The extreme and prolonged geomagnetic storms brought widespread middle and even low latitude aurorae with them on October 29 and 30. Aurora sightings occurred from California to Texas to Florida.
takeaway_quote: Keep your car’s gas tank at least half full. Gas stations rely on electricity to power their pumps.

place: New Jersey and the East Coast
event: Sandy made landfall in New Jersey; about 8.5 million customers lost power.
takeaway: Keep your phone charged before a storm, and buy backup chargers.
event_quote: Sandy damaged or destroyed at least 650,000 houses and left approximately 8.5 million customers without power during the storm and its aftermath.
takeaway_quote: Keep your cell phone charged when you know a hurricane is in the forecast and purchase backup charging devices to power electronics.

event: The Northeast blackout affected 30 million people.
takeaway: Find out if your home phone works in an outage and how long its battery lasts.
event_quote: This disturbance resulted in the loss of over 20,000 MW of load and affected 30 million people.
takeaway_quote: Determine whether your home phone will work in a power outage and how long battery backup will last.

event: The FCC and FEMA ran the first nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System.
takeaway: Pack a battery or hand-crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert.
event_quote: On November 9, 2011, at 2:00 p.m. Eastern Standard Time (EST), the FCC and FEMA conducted a nationwide test of the EAS. This event marked the first time the EAS (or its predecessor the Emergency Broadcast System (EBS)) had been tested on a nationwide basis.
takeaway_quote: Battery-powered or hand crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert
